newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn presents energy bill ahead of talks with SPD.
newsitem.headline: Bonn presents energy bill ahead of talks with SPD.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt on Thursday presented a long-delayed bill to open Germany's energy markets to competition, just ahead of talks with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) aimed at seeking consensus on energy policy controversies.
Although Rexrodt has been an outspoken champion of energy market liberalisation at the European level, the German bill is much less ambitious than his earlier plans.
Vehement domestic opposition from large utilities and small local governments has forced delays and compromises.

Still, at the first parliamentary reading of the bill, aimed at breaking up regional monopolies in Germany's first energy sector reform since 1935, Rexrodt said it would cut prices by up to 25 percent, secure jobs and reduce pollution.
The bill seeks to bring German law into line with last year's European Union resolution to open up energy markets to competition from vendors in other countries.

"Our electricity prices in the business sector are 20 to 30 percent higher than in important neighbouring countries," Rexrodt told parliament. "The lack of experience in competition weakens the German energy sector's international position."

The bill would also require local governments to provide rights of way for new gas and electricity lines but Rexrodt was forced to give ground on the idea of "negotiated third-party access", which would have forced owners of existing power lines to give competitors access to their networks.

The SPD and environmentalist Greens immediately attacked the watered-down bill, saying the government had fallen short of its own goals. The two opposition parties have drafted rival bills but they have little hope of passage.
SPD parliamentarian Volker Jung said Rexrodt's bill was targeted against local governments and "ecologically blind".

Small, independent power producers are hardly likely to build their own supply networks and real competition will only be achieved when they have "discrimination-free" access to existing networks, Jung said.

Greens energy spokeswoman Michaele Hustedt said the government had caved in to the power of Germany's eight major electric utilities and that its reform would not give small power suppliers a real chance.
The VIK energy industry association urged parliament to pass the government bill and not make it a political football.
"What German industry really needs today is quick and above all effective measures to improve the conditions of production. Electricity and gas costs are a decisive factor," VIK said in a statement.
"A further watering down of the proposal would be a clear decision against Germany as a manufacturing site," VIK said.
Rexrodt, Environment Minister Angela Merkel and Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl were to hold more talks with SPD leaders on Thursday night to address energy policy differences.
The SPD was to be represented by Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder and party manager Franz Muentefering. Utilities executives were also invited to attend the session.

The SPD, which opposes nuclear power, wants the government to start work on a nuclear waste dump in southern Germany, which has a high concentration of nuclear power plants, to relieve the pressure on the Gorleben site in northern Germany.
